steps.text: Teacher Song Ning brought rubbings of the two pet footprints we looked at yesterday, in a safe clearing on the Farm. They're here on this desk.
One's round, and one drags a bit of mud. I didn't chase after them. I just drew the leaves beside them to compare.
Our teacher says you can't tell which animal it was from one footprint. Anything I didn't see clearly gets a question mark.
Can you help me pick what to record first? We'll look at both, then put the rubbings back in the class folder.

choice.text: Compare the sizes first, and draw the leaves beside them.
choice.reply: Okay! With something to compare the size to, we won't have to guess next time.

choice.text: Check which way the footprints point, then write the date.
choice.reply: Okay! I'll draw the direction clearly, and I won't forget the date.

steps.text: My map is missing a bit of line between the school and South Street. The little muddy slope I drew gets hard to walk after rain.
Teacher Song Ning took us around by the public trail and checked there were railings and places to rest all along it.
On this class route card, both turns are checked. Paths nobody's checked stay dotted, and they're not for shortcuts.
Help me pick how to mark it, so even first-timers know which safe way to go.

choice.text: Draw a line of arrows along the public trail.
choice.reply: Okay! I'll run the arrows all the way to the school gate, with no gaps at the turns.

choice.text: Draw a bold mark at each of the two turns.
choice.reply: Okay! Next to both marks, I'll write "Walk with a grown-up."

steps.text: Our teacher put my little icons in the corner of the map! Footprints mean observation notes, and a little house means a place to rest.
They just help people find the way. Dangerous spots keep their old warnings, and the icons don't cover them up at all.
Neighbours who come to class can see this page. I'd like you to keep a copy of how to draw them in your own notes, too.
Let's fill in the last box of the legend! Should we draw a bench for resting first, or a little school book?

choice.text: The bench first, so tired walkers can find it easily.
choice.reply: Okay! I'll draw the bench nice and wide, with room to walk past.

choice.text: The book first, so people coming to class can find their way.
choice.reply: Okay! And I'll write the school's opening hours beside it.

dialogue.firstMeet: I'm Song Ning, and I teach at the School. In nature class there's no rush to learn every plant. First we learn to describe clearly what we see. If you've noticed things in your fields, come share them.

spring: New leaves and old leaves aren't the same color. That's where today's observation starts.
A specimen card can show a living plant. There's no need to pick it.
A child asked why seeds sleep so long. I wrote that question into my lesson notes, too.
Before holding class by a field, we ask the owner first and check the paths are passable.
Look at the same flower again a few days later, and slowly your notes gain a before and after.
summer: We start outdoor lessons early and head back to the Classroom once the sun is high.
To study reflections in the water, there's no need to reach past the railing.
Today everyone describes the edge of a leaf. Just writing "pretty" doesn't count.
I've left time for breaks in class. If you're tired, it's fine to say so.
Summer insect songs are lovely to record. Listen quietly for a while and you'll find something.
autumn: We borrow fallen leaves to observe, and once we're done they go back somewhere suitable.
The same crop grows differently in different fields. A good chance to talk about care.
Answers in class don't need to be tidy. An honest record is more useful than a lucky guess.
This harvest season, I'd like a farmer to share some experiences. Only if they're willing.
I've set out the old specimen cards so everyone can find this year's changes for themselves.
winter: We can't go far in the snow, but the light by the window is enough for an observation lesson.
Today we're comparing tree shadows from three seasons. You can see all four from the Classroom, too.
If you don't know a word, draw it. A drawing is a sincere way of saying something, too.
The children want to draw next year's fields. First I asked them to leave the paths wide enough.
The textbooks are mended. I left the folded corners, though. Those are the pages people turn to most.

rain: We're using indoor observation cards today. We'll go out and check once the paths dry.
Just wipe the mud off your shoes. You can tell me why you're late in your own time.

0: Start with something you've seen.
If you borrow observation cards from the School, remember to write the return date.
200: Your notes were so specific, the children could follow them and observe again.
Leaving blank space on a card is good. Whoever comes later has room to add.
400: Rainy-day lessons have two plans now, so I don't have to hurry everyone along at the last minute.
You pointing out what doesn't work in class helps more than a polite compliment.
600: Before I use any of your farm experiences, I'll always check that you're willing.
It's good for the children to know a farm has its uncertain moments too.

gift.love: This flower is perfect for an observation card. Thank you. I'll note where it came from, too.
gift.like: Thank you. This can go in the class's seasonal records.
gift.neutral: Thank you for the thought. I'd love to hear what you've seen lately, too.
gift.dislike: Thank you, but odds and ends like this don't really belong in a classroom.

dialogue.birthday: I've tucked today's birthday wishes into my lesson notes. The next page is saved for tomorrow's questions, as always.

festival.flower_fair: Observe the flower before you flip the sign. A wrong guess still adds a new note.
festival.fishing_derby: The children watching are all behind the safety line. Noting the colors of the fish is fun, too.
festival.picnic: If everyone tells where one ingredient came from, this meal becomes a nature lesson.
festival.firefly: You can sketch where the lanterns are. Tonight, adults will walk the trail with the children.
festival.market: Leave an observation card by each exhibit, so later visitors have questions to ask, too.
festival.harvest_coop: Light and heavy tasks are kept separate. Helping isn't measured by how strong you are.
festival.snow_craft: The children can build however they like. First, they learn where the borrowed wood pieces go back.
festival.hearth_night: If you didn't follow part of a story, ask. No need to rush to sum it up for the teller.

steps.text: Here are drawings of three common plants. The plants themselves stayed by the field. Today we'll make specimen cards from the drawings.
Write flower shape, leaf edge and date separately. If you're unsure of a name, leave it blank for now, so a guess doesn't become the answer.
These class cards stay here. Put them back in the folder when you're done. Nothing comes out of your Backpack.
Why don't you choose how to arrange them, so the children can use the cards to find the plants again?

choice.text: Lay out the three leaf drawings first, then add notes one by one.
choice.reply: Good. See what's alike and what's different first, then find words for what you noticed.

choice.text: Arrange them by date, with a column for changes.
choice.reply: Good. Come back in a while and we can keep adding notes.

steps.text: This is the record of our rainy-day backup lesson. The mud on the planned route hadn't dried, so we held class indoors that day.
Some children worried it wouldn't count without living plants, so we set the windowsill pot plants beside our earlier cards.
Everyone found two differences in the records. Once the paths are safe, adults will go along to check. No rushing up muddy slopes.
Next time the weather's like this, should we compare leaf shapes first, or have everyone share how they observed?

choice.text: Compare leaf shapes first, so everyone gets to pick up a pencil.
choice.reply: Good. With cards laid out on the table, even children who haven't been to the fields can join in.

choice.text: Take turns sharing how they observed, then check the cards together.
choice.reply: Good. Hearing different experiences teaches them to ask why.

steps.text: Nature class now has a farm story for background, about caring, observing and trying again when problems come up.
We'll only use your farm experiences if you want us to. If you'd rather not be named, we'll use a general example with no source.
Either way, it's the same lesson. The children won't need to visit your fields, and your usual days won't be disturbed.
How would you like this lesson's background to be kept?

choice.text: You can use my farm. Just show me what you'll say first.
choice.reply: Of course. I'll give you the draft to check before I plan the lesson.

choice.text: Use a general example. I'd like to keep farm life to myself.
choice.reply: Of course. Your personal experiences stay out of class. We'll explain it with public records.

dialogue.firstMeet: I'm Bai Lu. I usually paint in the Community Hall. No need to rush to name a painting. Whatever spot catches your eye, let's start talking from there.

spring: Fresh green is so bright that, when I paint it, I keep a little gray in.
Not all the flowers are out yet. Bare branches are worth painting too.
The light slants in from the street corner today. I want to wait while it drifts over to the door.
Before I paint the field paths, I make sure I know where people walk.
The same view at a different hour is like the same words in a different tone of voice.
summer: My Honey Drink's in the shade. I'll have it after this stroke.
Afternoon shadows are short, so the open ground in the picture looks bigger.
Lantern light needn't be painted exactly. First, remember how it falls on the water.
I want to try leaving out one color, and see if the painting still holds together.
That cloud you described... I still haven't found a color that can catch it.
autumn: Fall isn't only gold. The blue on wet stones runs deep, too.
The hardest thing to paint at a market is the moment someone decides to stop.
Walk a place you've painted once more, and you'll always spot what you missed.
Today I'm painting just one stretch of field path, not cramming the whole valley in.
The way leaves pile against the wall looks more natural than anything I could arrange.
winter: Snow softens every sound, near and far. A painting can leave space empty too.
If I move the easel over a little, everyone can sit around the bench in the Community Hall.
When your hands are cold, have something warm first. No need to force a painting.
I looked through last winter's sketches. Back then I always wanted to fill every corner.
The new painting has no name yet. I'll let it hang on the wall a few days first.

rain: Rain blurs the colors together. I'll draw the outlines first and sort them out later.
The light indoors changes too. Today I'll just watch it slowly from the easel.

0: You don't have to judge a painting. Just tell me where your eyes stopped.
There's a free seat by the easel if you're tired from walking.
200: The colors you picked made me see the same street all over again.
I'm keeping both sketches. Neither has to make way for the other.
400: This time I narrowed the subject, and the painting can finally breathe.
That detail you pointed out did more than a pretty sky ever could.
600: Since the paintings went up in the Community Hall, I often stand back and listen to people talk.
That landscape belongs here. I only held on to what I saw for a little while.

gift.love: The color and the scent are both just right. Thank you.
gift.like: Thank you. Today's observations just gained one more little clue.
gift.neutral: I'll take it. Next time, coming empty-handed to talk about painting is nice too.
gift.dislike: Thanks, but Coal and odds and ends like these don't belong on my painting table.

dialogue.birthday: Today I'm giving myself half a day off. I'll take a small sheet of paper out with me, with no rule about what it becomes.

festival.flower_fair: Even one kind of flower comes in lighter and darker shades. I want to paint them side by side.
festival.fishing_derby: Every ripple on the river is different. Just watching keeps me busy.
festival.picnic: The picnic cloth makes the food look brighter. I'll eat first, then paint.
festival.firefly: The three lantern lights needn't look alike. The water adds its own stroke.
festival.market: Leave a little empty space on the stall, so visitors know where to start looking.
festival.harvest_coop: Once the flower boxes are set, I'd like to paint people sitting down after the hauling's done.
festival.snow_craft: I'm using two close colors for my snow scene. Even from afar, you can tell front from back.
festival.hearth_night: Tonight I'll just listen to stories. The sketch paper can wait until tomorrow.

steps.text: I did two small sketches of the same corner of the Town Square. Same outlines, one in warm colors, one in cool.
The warm one is like a sunny afternoon, the cool one like a cloud just covering the sun. It's a color exercise, so no need to wait for the weather to change.
I'm keeping both. I'd like to hear which one shows you the everyday life you know first.
You choose which one I finish today. I'll take my time with the other later.

choice.text: The warm one. Keep that wooden stool sunning by the window.
choice.reply: All right. If the warmth sits on the stool, the walls don't all have to glow too.

choice.text: The cool one. Let the quiet of the corner show.
choice.reply: All right. Give the shadows a few layers. Quiet has its own color, too.

steps.text: Exhibit sketches cover half the table. Field paths, Riverside, the street corner... I wanted them all, and now you can't tell what I'm really looking at.
I've put the Riverside one in my folder for now. This time I'll pick either the field path or the corner, and look closely.
Whichever I pick gets its own place. The other subject can wait. It doesn't have to be given up forever for this show.
Where would you like to rest your eyes with me?

choice.text: The field path. See how footsteps wore the dirt trail in.
choice.reply: All right. The path and the grassy edges first. The far-off hills can wait.

choice.text: The street corner. See where neighbours stop.
choice.reply: All right. I'll paint the doorways and the bench clearly. There don't need to be many people.

steps.text: The subject we settled on last time is finished. The Community Hall hung that original landscape on this wall.
I left the sketches beside it, so everyone can see how it went from wanting to paint everything to truly looking at one place.
There's space left in front of it, so you can see it clearly sitting down, without squeezing behind the easel.
The label card still has one empty line. Should it be the date I observed it, or the name of the place?

choice.text: The date, so people remember the season.
choice.reply: All right. The view will keep changing. A date gives this one moment of seeing a place to land.

choice.text: The place name, so passersby recognize their own lives.
choice.reply: All right. Once they recognize it, maybe they'll tell me about their own picture of it.

dialogue.firstMeet: Wen Heng. I keep the archives. If the valley you remember differs from what's on paper, please tell me. I check the source first, then decide how to fill the gap.

spring: Waterlines shift. The date on the back of a photo is more useful than you'd think.
The new observation notes still have mud on them. I'll lay them on paper to dry first.
The handwriting on a seed packet is a record of this season, too.
I won't erase the question marks on the old map. Notes get added once there's evidence.
Someone remembers which rock the spring water reached. I kept their exact words beside it.
summer: It's humid. Don't store pages against the wall.
That one ferry crossing has two old names. We can't keep only the one we know better.
Envelopes from the Waystation are dated, but what's inside didn't necessarily happen that day.
Summer brings lots of records. I sort them by source, so hearsay and measurements don't get mixed.
You can describe the river's color, but a color can't stand in for a water level.
autumn: The small corrections in a harvest ledger say more about the year's hardships than the totals.
When a stall label says where something came from, even an ordinary thing is worth a look.
I set the new map beside the old photos and look first for points that surely haven't changed.
Leaves pressed in a book leave marks. When I take one out, I make a separate note.
Someone corrected one of my transcriptions today. This page is finally a bit more reliable.
winter: Old paper turns brittle. Turn the pages slowly. No need to hurry through.
Winter is good for sorting oral accounts. The parts the speaker wasn't sure of stay in, too.
Keep photos from before and after the rebuilding, so "change" isn't just an empty word.
Not every blank needs filling. Some things simply aren't known yet.
This year's index is finished. It can still be corrected next year.

rain: Leave your wet umbrella by the door. There's already a dry mat on the records table.
You can hear the rain clearly. Just right for checking a few oral accounts line by line.

0: Even if I can't find it, you'll get an answer. I won't fill in with guesses.
Please keep borrowed photos on the table. And don't miss the writing on the back.
200: For the two waterlines you checked, I noted the evidence beside the index.
The old photo finally has a date we can trace. Future searches will be easier.
400: The correction page sits with the old one, so how the mistake came about is kept too.
When you disagreed with that note, you gave your evidence. I appreciate that.
600: The comparison exhibit now has a page of your observations. Name and source both checked.
The archive will keep growing. Life today is worth recording carefully too.

gift.love: This mineral deserves a close look. If you remember where it came from, let's write it on a card together.
gift.like: Thank you. Useful for observation and comparison.
gift.neutral: Received. I'll put it somewhere appropriate.
gift.dislike: Thank you, but things like this would soil the records. They can't go in the archive cabinet.

dialogue.birthday: Today I'm not fact-checking anyone's write-up about me. A cup of hot water and one small thing you saw firsthand is just right.

festival.flower_fair: If the flower signs note their source, next year we can look back and see which ones stayed.
festival.fishing_derby: Results are a record. The weather and how people took part should go in too.
festival.picnic: Home dishes often go by different names. I'd like to note them all alongside.
festival.firefly: The lantern spots go on today's map, but it's not a survey of the river.
festival.market: When you collect your exhibit, check it against the loan form. The Market Medallion is logged separately in your Collection.
festival.harvest_coop: Sorting counts and the helpers' list are written separately, so neither goods nor people get left out.
festival.snow_craft: Photograph the finished snow scene, and return the borrowed wood pieces by count.
festival.hearth_night: For stories people want kept, I ask the teller first, then write them up as records.

steps.text: I found this old photo of the waterways in a lending ledger. The original stays in the Archive. We'll work from the protective copy on the table.
Two pencil lines on the back point to the water inlet and the old footpath. The date gives only a season, so we can't treat it as an exact year.
Uncle An's account and the project records are beside it. We mark what can be verified first, and the rest stays open.
Which line do you want to check first? Once both are done, the copy goes back in the archive folder.

choice.text: The inlet first, then the footpath's position.
choice.reply: Good. Start with a fixed structure, and the second line gains a reference point.

choice.text: The old footpath first, then back to the inlet.
choice.reply: Good. Start from where people walked. The waterline still needs its own evidence.

steps.text: On this map, a side channel was copied down as the main channel, and several later notes repeated the same mistake.
We've laid out the photo's two lines, the oral account and the project records. The parts that back each other up are circled.
A correction doesn't mean pulling the old page. I keep the original, the date of the change and the evidence, so later readers know why.
Should the correction notice start with the photo, or with the project records?

choice.text: The photo first, so people can see the two original lines.
choice.reply: Good. Underneath, I'll state that the date is unconfirmed. Missing evidence doesn't become certainty.

choice.text: List the project records first, then explain how the old map was miscopied.
choice.reply: Good. Every correction can be traced to a source, and the original page stays available.

steps.text: The before-and-after rebuilding exhibit is set up. The old waterlines and today's routes each have a column, and anything unconfirmed keeps its note.
Contributors' records are listed by source, so everyone's work isn't reduced to a single project figure.
The comparison maps use the same reference points. You can see what changed, and the life that didn't.
There's room for a reading tip at the top. Should it remind people to check the dates first, or to find the reference points?

choice.text: Check the dates, then read the changes.
choice.reply: Good. Records from different times each keep their place, so before and after never get flipped.

choice.text: Find the shared reference points, then follow the waterways.
choice.reply: Good. Once readers know where they are, they can take their time reading their own valley.

dialogue.firstMeet: Folks round here call me Granny Shi, and so can you. I've walked plenty of the old waterways. Some I don't recall so well, but let's sit and talk it over.

spring: Spring water used to wind round that rock. Where it runs now, you'll have to go see for yourself, from somewhere safe.
Don't toss all the tender greens in the pot at once. Think which ones can take the cooking.
The ground's warming up. No need for an extra cushion on the bench now.
A new road's not good just for being wide. It's good if these old legs can manage it.
When flowers bloom, let them be. You can enjoy them for days just passing by.
summer: Hot soup can wait a moment. Catching your breath won't hold up the work.
Sit in the shade come afternoon. Toughing it out in the sun doesn't make you a hard worker.
My old fan still works fine, and the new windows let the air through. Each has its use.
I go see the lanterns by the river with the neighbours, and we come home along the lit path.
Salt can always be fixed. Have a little taste first, then decide.
autumn: This year's vegetables taste of this year. They needn't match the old days.
Don't leave the empty baskets by the door after harvest. Folks with carts need to get by.
The new flower boxes look lovely. Nudge them to the side a bit and they'd be handier still.
Don't go just praising the old days, mind. Travelling the waterways back then was far more bother than now.
Sweep the leaves into one pile, so folks by the bench keep their shoes clean.
winter: Warm the soup bowls on cold days, so there's still steam when they reach the table.
When the snow's deep, don't play the hero. Wait till the path's cleared.
When stories go round the hearth and you miss a bit, ask them to say it again. No need to pretend.
This year brought plenty of new things, and a few more folks willing to sit a while.
Winter's long. Work meant for tomorrow can be set down today.

rain: Heavy rain? Come in and sit. Old waterway stories tell just as well in here.
The benches in the Community Hall are nice and dry. When the roads are slick, we move our gathering there.

0: If you've something to say, sit down and say it. Standing in the doorway gets in folks' way.
Knowing the old roads doesn't mean I needn't ask about the new ones.
200: You take a moment when you taste the soup. That's how you get a feel for the salt.
There's no secret to this home-style soup. If you fancy it, try another pot.
400: You didn't mind my chatter, and you were willing to look the path over again.
Old habits worth keeping, we keep. The awkward ones, we change together.
600: There's a spot at the bench gathering where you can stretch your legs. If you're busy, come next time.
My wish isn't long: may folks here walk easy, and always find a seat.

gift.love: That's the taste of home, just right. Thank you. Let it cool a touch, then we'll talk.
gift.like: Thank you. Things that help you live well are the real deal.
gift.neutral: I'll take it. Next time, come sit empty-handed, that's fine too.
gift.dislike: Thanks for thinking of me, but raw fish doesn't agree with me. Cooked home food suits me better.

dialogue.birthday: Even at seventy, you live it one meal at a time. I'll set out an extra chair today. Anyone free, come sit.

festival.flower_fair: I still remember this flower's old name. Read me the new one, too.
festival.fishing_derby: Come sit after the derby. No bites won't spoil the festival.
festival.picnic: The food needn't be fancy. Everyone eating comfortably is what counts.
festival.firefly: I walk the lit trail with the neighbours, and when I tire, I watch from a bench.
festival.market: Put out ordinary household things too, so folks can see how everyday life goes.
festival.harvest_coop: I'll leave the heavy work to others. Sitting and sorting these greens helps all the same.
festival.snow_craft: Leave a flat path to the snow house door, so visitors can get in.
festival.hearth_night: A light gift's no matter. Taking the trouble to send your greetings is what gives it weight.

steps.text: The Clear Broth's off the stove and on the little table by my rattan chair. Today's lesson is about heat. I won't take any ingredients from you.
Wash the Wild Greens before they go in, and add the quick-cooking ones later. Go easy on salt. You can add more after tasting.
In the old days every home's pot was different. Even the same traditional soup had its own way in each house.
Once this bowl's cooled a bit, will you smell it first, or take a little sip to check the salt?

choice.text: Smell it first, then have a little taste.
choice.reply: Good. Remember the aroma and the saltiness separately, and next time you'll know.

choice.text: A little taste first, then say which green stands out.
choice.reply: Good. No rush to answer. Your tongue needs time to sort out the flavors too.

steps.text: I always kept my bucket by the door, but now the new carts have to go round it. Nearly had another squabble over it yesterday.
New things that save effort are good, and old habits can move too. So first we measured the path in front of the door.
There's a flat way in and out by the bench now. Sunny days we sit on South Street, rainy days in the Community Hall, so folks with bad legs don't come for nothing.
Help me think how to word the gathering invitation so the neighbours get it easily.

choice.text: Start with the place and the step-free path.
choice.reply: Right. Anyone who wants to come should know the way first. I'll move that bucket inside.

choice.text: Say it moves to the Community Hall on rainy days, then add the time.
choice.reply: Good. No one should be hunting for a chair in the rain. Place and time, both written out.

steps.text: The bench gathering's all arranged. South Street when it's sunny, the Community Hall when it rains. This time I sent the invitations out first.
After sitting a while, folks said the new road has places to rest now, and old neighbours bump into each other more.
I wrote my wish for the Town's changes on this card: may folks here walk easy, and always find a seat.
Before I take the card to the bench, have a look for me. Should I write bigger, or leave a space for others to add to?

choice.text: Write bigger, so it can be read sitting down.
choice.reply: All right. I'll trace it out slow and clear, so nobody has to lean in close.

choice.text: Leave a space for the neighbours to add to.
choice.reply: All right. My line goes first, and everyone can write the days that follow.
